juju · Phase 9 · Scale and hardening

When juju says "got it", the event is safe

Until now, an event ingest had accepted waited in memory for a worker. Restart the server at the wrong moment and it was gone, though the SDK had been told it arrived and had deleted its copy. Phase 9 puts a durable queue between ingest and the workers. It adds limits so one noisy app can't flood the server, removes personal data before anything is written, and deletes data once it's old.

[phase 9] DONE verified="kill -9 mid-flood: 0 of 57,700 accepted events lost (main lost 4,237 of 60,511); p99 1.3–21 ms at 5,000 events/s in four runs; Postgres down: ingest kept answering 202, event stored 17 s after it came back" tests="Go unit + integration (Postgres, ClickHouse, JetStream), 2 fuzzers, 165 JS, 74 Flutter"
The durable queue

202 is a promise

Ingest answers 202 Accepted, and the SDK then deletes the event from its own queue. From that moment juju is the only place the event exists. So 202 must mean "this will be stored", not "this is in a Go channel and will be stored unless the process dies first".

The test: flood the server for 20 seconds from 16 threads, kill -9 it 6 seconds in (no chance to shut down cleanly), start it again, and compare every event id that got a 202 with the ids in the database.

Before: main, in-memory channel 4,237 lost

60,511 events got a 202. 4,237 of them (7%) were in memory when the process died and never reached Postgres.

After: Phase 9, JetStream on disk 0 lost

57,700 events got a 202, and 57,700 are stored: none missing, none twice. The restarted server found waiting: 3956 in the queue and stored them all.

How it works

  • The queue is NATS JetStream, embedded in the juju binary and stored in JUJU_DATA_DIR/queue. A single server needs no new service to install or run.
  • Ingest answers 202 only after JetStream has acknowledged storing the event (PubAck).
  • A worker acknowledges an event only after it is in Postgres. If it crashes holding one, JetStream hands that event to a worker again after 30 s.
  • Each message carries the event's id as Nats-Msg-Id, so an SDK retrying the same batch within 2 minutes isn't queued twice. Postgres's primary key catches anything later.
  • A failing event is retried after 1 s, 5 s, 30 s, then every minute. After 50 tries it goes to a dead-letter stream (JUJU_DEAD, kept for 7 days) instead of blocking the queue forever.
Why JetStream, not Redis StreamsBoth were on the roadmap. JetStream runs inside the Go binary, which keeps the one-server deploy at exactly one process plus Postgres. When ingest and workers need to be separate machines, the same code connects to a standalone NATS server instead. Redis would have been a new service to install, secure and back up on day one.
Try it

What happens when…

    Measured

    p99 under 50 ms in every run

    The roadmap's target: ingest keeps its 99th-percentile response under 50 ms at a target rate. The test is k6 with a constant arrival rate: it starts requests on schedule whether or not earlier ones have answered. A closed loop, where each user waits for its reply, quietly slows down when the server does, and hides exactly the latency being measured. Each request is a batch of 10 errors, as an SDK flushes them.

    RunAcceptedp50p95p99Did the 2 workers keep up?
    5,000 events/s, 30 s
    first run, 0.4M rows    		100%0.42 ms0.74 ms2.2 msYes: the queue stayed empty
    20,000 events/s, 20 s
    4× the target    		100%0.41 ms3.6 ms15 msNo, and that's the point: they stored ~3,200/s, the rest waited on disk (221 MB) and all 398,680 were stored 77 s after the end
    5,000 events/s, 60 s
    final code, load average 13    		100%0.39 ms1.9 ms21 msNot quite: 74% stored live, the rest from the queue right after
    5,000 events/s, 30 s
    final code, 1.1M rows, load average 10–12    		100%0.35 ms0.56 ms1.3 msNot quite: 83% live, 18 MB queued, all 150,010 stored right after

    Ingest doesn't wait for Postgres at all, which is why its latency barely moves when the workers fall behind. The workers are the real limit. They slowed down as the table grew past a million rows and gained an index (each insert updates every index), on a laptop busy with other work. When that happens, events wait on disk instead of being refused or lost, and JUJU_WORKERS or another worker process adds throughput.

    Measured on an 8-core MacBook with k6, juju and Postgres on the same machine, and other programs running (load average 10–13 in the last two runs). The 21 ms run was the busiest. A dedicated server should do better, but these are the numbers measured. Run it yourself with make loadtest.

    Split deployment

    Ingest, workers and the dashboard can run apart

    One process runs everything by default. JUJU_ROLES picks the parts, so ingest can scale on its own, or a slow dashboard query can't touch the endpoint apps send to:

    # three processes, one shared NATS JetStream server (nats-server -js)
JUJU_ROLES=ingest      JUJU_NATS_URL=nats://nats:4222 juju serve  # POST /api/v1/.../events only
JUJU_ROLES=worker      JUJU_NATS_URL=nats://nats:4222 juju serve  # stores events, alerts, retention
JUJU_ROLES=api         JUJU_NATS_URL=nats://nats:4222 juju serve  # dashboard and read API

    Live updates travel the same way. The worker that stores an event publishes juju.live.<project> on NATS, and every API process passes it to the browsers watching that project. Before, this only worked inside one process: Phase 7's limits listed it as not done yet.

    Why it refuses to start without NATSThe embedded queue lives inside one process. JUJU_ROLES=ingest on its own would queue events that no worker can ever see. juju exits at startup with the reason instead of accepting events it will never store.
    Rate limits and quotas

    One app can't take the server down for everyone

    An app stuck in an error loop on a million phones can send more than the server stores. Each project gets two limits:

    • A rate limit (default 1,000 events/s) as a token bucket. Tokens refill at the rate, up to 5 seconds' worth, and each event spends one. The burst is there because SDKs send in batches, and a phone that was offline sends its backlog all at once.
    • A monthly quota (none by default), counted in Postgres as events accepted per calendar month.

    Over either one, ingest answers 429 with Retry-After, and all three SDKs already keep the events and wait that long. The rate limit asks for the seconds until enough tokens are back. The quota asks for one hour, not "next month", so a raised quota takes effect within the hour.

    $ juju project limits -id 1 -rate 10
  rate limit: 10 events/s
$ # 100 events (the burst), then 5 more right away, then 5 after a second
202 {"accepted":100}
429 Retry-After: 1 {"error":"rate limit exceeded"}
202 {"accepted":5}
    Why a refused batch gives its tokens backWhen the queue itself refuses a batch, the SDK will resend it. If the tokens stayed spent, the same events would use the allowance twice. A test caught this: the test expected Retry-After: 1 and got 3.
    Why counts are flushed, not written per requestUpdating a usage row on every request would make one Postgres row the hottest spot in the system. Ingest counts in memory and adds to project_usage every 5 seconds and at shutdown. Adding, not setting, is what lets several ingest processes share one count.
    PII scrubbing

    Personal data is removed before it's written anywhere

    Apps send personal data by accident all the time: an email in an error message, a password-reset token in a URL a breadcrumb recorded, an Authorization header copied into context. juju removes it at ingest, before the queue, so it never reaches the queue's files, Postgres or ClickHouse. Scrubbing in the worker would have left it sitting in the queue on disk.

    WhereSentStored
    Error messageno account for grace.hopper@navy.milno account for [email]
    Breadcrumb URL…/session?access_token=abc123secret&next=/cart…/session?access_token=[Filtered]&next=/cart
    Context headerAuthorization: Bearer sk_live_9f8e…Authorization: [Filtered]
    user.emailgrace.hopper@navy.milgrace.hopper@navy.mil (kept: set on purpose)

    It also catches JWTs, OAuth ?code=, S3 signatures, and any value under keys like password, cookie or api_key. It leaves alone the fields an app fills in to say who the user is (user.*, distinct_id), stack frames, and look-alikes: @babel/core, /tokenizer?mode=fast, "the bearer of bad news". Each event records how many values were scrubbed, never what they were. A fuzzer checks that scrubbing never crashes and that a second pass finds nothing left.

    Retention

    Old data is deleted on a schedule

    • Postgres: error events, app sessions, transactions and alert deliveries older than JUJU_RETENTION_DAYS (90) are deleted every hour, along with expired logins and invites. Issues stay, with their counts, so an old bug that comes back is still recognised as a regression.
    • ClickHouse: analytics events older than JUJU_ANALYTICS_RETENTION_DAYS (365) are dropped by ClickHouse itself, through a table TTL.
    Why 5,000 rows at a timeOne huge DELETE holds its locks and writes WAL for minutes while ingest is writing to the same tables. Small batches each finish in milliseconds. A Postgres advisory lock means that with several workers only one deletes, and the others skip that hour instead of fighting over the same rows.
    Why the new indexes are built CONCURRENTLYDeleting by age needs an index on the time column. A plain CREATE INDEX blocks writes for as long as it builds, so the deploy that adds it would stall ingest. CONCURRENTLY builds it alongside writes. On the test database it took 0.85 s for 808,000 events.
    Using it

    Defaults that are safe, and the knobs

    Nothing to do for a single server: the queue is embedded, and the defaults below apply. They go in /etc/juju/juju.env:

    SettingDefaultWhat it does
    JUJU_RATE_LIMIT1000events/s per project without its own limit; 0 turns the default off
    JUJU_RETENTION_DAYS90errors, sessions, transactions; 0 keeps them
    JUJU_ANALYTICS_RETENTION_DAYS365analytics events in ClickHouse; 0 keeps them
    JUJU_SCRUB_PIItruefalse stores events exactly as sent
    JUJU_QUEUE_MAX_MB1024queue size on disk; past it, ingest answers 429
    JUJU_ANALYTICS_QUEUE_MAX_MB512analytics events waiting for ClickHouse; past it, the oldest are dropped and ingest keeps answering
    JUJU_ROLESingest,worker,apiwhich parts this process runs
    JUJU_NATS_URL(embedded)a shared NATS JetStream; needed to split roles
    JUJU_TRUSTED_PROXIES127.0.0.1,::1proxies whose X-Forwarded-For is believed, so login and sign-up limits see each visitor's real address
     
    # per project; a flag left out keeps its value, no flags just shows them
juju project limits -id 1 -rate 500 -quota 5000000
juju project limits -id 1 -rate default -quota none

// SDKs: send a share of errors (sessions still count every one)
juju.init({ dsn, sampleRate: 0.25 })                     // web, React Native
Juju.init(JujuOptions(dsn: dsn, sampleRate: 0.25))       // Flutter
    Why sessions are never sampledThe crash-free rate is crashed sessions over all sessions. Sample those and the rate is wrong. So sampleRate drops error reports, while the session still counts the error. Analytics events aren't sampled either: a funnel built from a quarter of its steps isn't a funnel.

    What was checked

    Against a running juju with Postgres, with the queue on disk, and every result read back from the database.

    What testing exposed

    sessions that never became healthy

    The Phase 8 end-to-end test timed out. Fields the server computes (a session's start, a transaction's start) are marked json:"-", so they vanished in the JSON trip through the queue. The old channel passed Go objects and hid it. Now they're rebuilt after the queue, and a test compares every field before and after.

    tokens spent twice

    A batch the queue refused still used up its rate-limit tokens, though the SDK would resend it. The test's Retry-After: 3 instead of 1 showed it. Refused batches now give their tokens back.

    503 during a database outage

    The first outage test got 503: checking the project key needed Postgres, which defeated the point of the queue. The cache now serves the last known project when Postgres can't be reached.

    "insufficient storage"

    JetStream reserves each stream's full size up front, so the dead-letter stream didn't fit next to the main one. The overall store limit is now only a high ceiling, and each stream's own limit is the real one, so lowering a limit can't stop the server from starting either.

    Limits

    Not covered yet

    • Power loss: a crash or kill -9 loses nothing, because the operating system still writes what JetStream handed it. A power cut can lose events accepted in roughly the last 2 minutes, which is JetStream's default interval for forcing data to disk. Syncing every write would cost latency on every request.
    • Rate limits are per ingest process: three ingest replicas allow up to three times a project's rate. The quota is shared, but each replica sees the others' counts only every few seconds.
    • Limits have no dashboard screen yet: set them with juju project limits.
    • Retention is one setting for the whole server, not per project, and ClickHouse drops data in whole months.
    • Stack frames aren't scrubbed: a signed CDN URL in a script's filename stays as sent, because source maps are matched by it.
    • One NATS server: a split deployment's queue is a single machine. A 3-node JetStream cluster would remove that, with no code change.
    • /readyz checks Postgres, so a load balancer would take an ingest-only process out of rotation during a database outage, even though it could keep accepting.
